observations: Hedge-token frequency stratifies sharply by topic-type across the 12 Part 1 responses in the full text transcript. Purely descriptive/factual answers (Q1 'where are you from', Q2 'work or student', Q12 'jobs in hometown') contain zero instances of 'probably', 'I think', 'I'd probably say', or 'in my opinion'. Their only softeners are 'Yeah, so' openers, 'just', 'you know' (1× in Q12), and 'things like that' (1× in Q12). By contrast, evaluative-preference answers (Q4 phone-vs-email, Q5 follow-up, Q7 travel, Q8 UK places, Q10 hometown-for-children) average 3.4 hedge tokens per response drawn from the set {probably, I think, I'd probably say, kind of, you know, in my opinion, as I feel like, a bit}. The sandwich-and-hedge architecture is therefore topic-triggered—activated specifically when the speaker must commit to a judgment, rank, or acknowledge a limitation—rather than a global discourse default that colors every turn regardless of epistemic demand.

The canonical sandwich (positive frame → subordinate limitation → positive re-affirmation) appears in exactly four responses: Q3 (call → if urgent, text → but usually call), Q7 (love traveling → only reason is time/money → but I love it), Q10 (children absolutely → teenagers not so much → but definitely children → younger children definitely), and Q6 (most annoying thing ever → I don't know it's true—a collapsed/inverted sandwich where the hedge follows the absolute rather than bracketing it). The remaining eight responses lack this three-part arc entirely. Q1, Q2, Q11 (historical narrative portion), and Q12 are linear descriptive enumerations with no limitation clause to bracket. This distribution confirms the sandwich is a response to the structural requirement of acknowledging a downside within an otherwise positive or assertive claim, not a universal turn-organization habit.

Within evaluative responses, the specific hedge tokens serve distinguishable pragmatic functions rather than a single undifferentiated 'uncertainty' signal. 'Probably' (7 total occurrences across Q5, Q7, Q8, Q10) operates as an epistemic attenuator on factual or ranking claims ('I've probably visited almost every place', 'London Bridge is probably my favorite'). 'I think / I'd probably say' (Q5, Q10) functions as a deference marker that explicitly hands interpretive authority back to the examiner ('I think I'd probably say', 'Teenagers I'd probably say not so much'). 'You know' (9 total across Q4, Q6, Q7, Q11, Q12) is a co-presence/validation check that invites the listener to confirm shared understanding, appearing in both evaluative AND descriptive turns—suggesting it is a baseline interpersonal habit distinct from the evaluative hedges. 'Kind of / a bit' (Q4) softens comparative judgments without bracketing. 'Things like that' (Q7, Q8, Q10, Q11, Q12) is an open-ended exemplification marker that avoids closing a list definitively. The functional heterogeneity of these tokens means a simple frequency count overstates uniformity; the sandwich specifically recruits 'probably', 'I think/I'd probably say', and the limitation-reaffirmation frame, while 'you know' and 'things like that' operate independently of the evaluative context.

The Q5 follow-up ('I really think it's just because you can't see their face um it's definitely just not the same I think I'd probably say') reveals a distinctive terminal-hedge pattern: after producing a confident sensory justification ('you can't see their face', 'it's definitely just not the same'), the speaker appends 'I think I'd probably say' as a trailing softener that retroactively undermines the preceding certainty. This is not a sandwich (no limitation clause) but a hedge-tail—a single epistemic retreat at the turn's end. The same pattern appears in Q6's collapse ('it's the most annoying thing ever I'll tell you that you know you hear the whole conversation you know what I mean it's I don't know it's true'), where the absolute superlative is immediately followed by 'I don't know' and a weak reassertion 'it's true'. These two instances suggest the speaker experiences discomfort with unqualified assertions and deploys a post-hoc hedge to protect his own face (avoiding appearing dogmatic) as well as the interlocutor's (leaving room for disagreement). However, this pattern is absent from purely descriptive turns, reinforcing that it is triggered by evaluative commitment rather than operating as a global default.

Comparing the examiner's authority framing across all 12 questions: every prompt is read from a scripted booklet in a flat procedural tone, with no personalization, no challenge, and no affective cue (confirmed across M1–M12 observations). The candidate's hedge density does NOT correlate with the examiner's perceived aggressiveness or authority level—because the examiner's behavior is invariant. Instead, hedge density correlates with the cognitive-evaluative demand of the question itself: 'Do you prefer X or Y?' (Q4, Q5) and 'Is it a good place?' (Q9, Q10) and 'What's your favorite?' (Q8) elicit 3+ hedges per turn, while 'Where are you from?' (Q1), 'Do you work or study?' (Q2), and 'What jobs do people do?' (Q12) elicit 0–1. This dissociation—constant authority framing, variable hedge output tied to question type—argues against the hypothesis that the sandwich is purely a response to the examiner as authority figure. If it were solely deference-to-authority, hedge density would be uniform across all questions. The topic-triggered distribution is more consistent with a stable interpersonal trait (discomfort with unqualified evaluative claims, preference for face-protective hedging around judgments) that is activated by the IELTS format's heavy sampling of opinion questions but is not manufactured by the examiner's presence alone.

The 'you know' co-presence marker (9 occurrences) and 'things like that' open-ended exemplifier (6 occurrences) appear in both evaluative and descriptive turns, including Q12 (purely enumerative: 'they'll grow you know a lot of vegetables... and things like that') and Q11 (historical narrative: 'old churches and shipwrecks and things like that'). This sequencing suggests the candidate's hedging is not a reflexive response to evaluative questions per se but is triggered specifically when he must articulate the STRUCTURE of his evaluation—concede limitations, rank alternatives, or acknowledge exceptions. A bare yes/no judgment ('absolutely') requires no face-protection because it commits to nothing beyond agreement with the examiner's implicit framing.
